Nordic Bank — Security + data retention / residency review (Redwood Inference)

Nordic Bank reviewed Redwood’s security posture with emphasis on EU data residency and strict retention controls. Customer asked for clear answers on what Redwood retains by default (prompts/responses, token/latency telemetry, logs) and how retention can be configured or disabled in Private/VPC. They also requested reporting by region and environment/tier (hosted vs dedicated vs private) to support governance and internal chargeback. Redwood outlined current capabilities (EU regions, private deployment options, RBAC/SSO, audit logs, configurable log retention) and noted that cost/unit-economics drilldowns by region/tier are currently internal but can be shared as aggregated summaries during pilot/QBRs. Next steps include sending security package (SOC2, ISO, pen test summary), a written retention matrix, and scheduling a follow-up focused on Redwood Private architecture and EU-only controls.
Data residency and regional processing controls (EU-only requirement)
Retention policy: prompts, responses, embeddings, and metadata/logs
Audit logging, RBAC, SSO/SAML, and access review
Redwood Private (VPC) vs Hosted API vs Dedicated capacity
Observability: metrics/logs/traces, PII handling, and customer-controlled exports
Cost transparency requests: region drilldowns and tiered reporting expectations
Redwood (Marcus) to send security package: SOC 2 report, ISO certificate, pen test executive summary, and subprocessor list
Redwood (Kaitlyn) to send SSO/SAML + RBAC overview and audit log event schema (sample payloads)
Redwood (Allison) to send data retention matrix (what’s stored where, default retention, and configuration knobs per deployment mode)
Nordic Bank (Priya) to share their required retention language and any DPA addendum clauses (EU SCCs, deletion SLAs, audit rights)
Schedule technical session on Redwood Private (VPC) EU-only routing, KMS integration, and log export patterns

[00:30] Sanna Kivinen: Yes. For us, residency and retention is the gating item. We can’t have prompts or responses leaving EU, and retention must be minimal, ideally zero on your side unless it’s required for service operation. 
[00:44] Marissa Cole: Understood. Just to anchor, Redwood supports EU regions for hosted, and for private we can deploy a VPC control plane with customer-managed networking. For strict requirements, most banks choose private. But let’s get more specific.

[01:03] Priya Nair: I’ll ask bluntly. Do you store customer prompts and completions? And for how long?
[01:10] Marcus Lin: Good question. By default, for our hosted API, we do process prompts and completions to generate responses, but we do not use them to train models. Regarding storage: we keep request metadata and operational logs for a bounded retention period. The raw prompt/response payload retention depends on logging settings—there are configurations to redact or not persist bodies. 
[01:34] Priya Nair: “Depends” makes me nervous. We need it written. 
[01:38] Marcus Lin: Totally fair. We can provide a retention matrix: what is stored, where, for what purpose, and the default retention. 
[01:45] Allison Grant: And from an observability perspective, we distinguish between: (1) payload content (prompt/response), (2) token counts and latency metrics, and (3) infrastructure logs. We can operate with payloads disabled, while still keeping metering like output token counts, request IDs, and timing. 

[02:05] Erik Lund: When you say “EU regions,” is it like Azure Sweden Central, Azure West Europe, that type? Or your own colo?
[02:12] Marissa Cole: For hosted, we’re on major cloud regions—think eu-west and eu-north equivalents—depending on the model and capacity. For Dedicated and Private we can pin to a specific region. We also have a region normalization layer internally, but practically: you choose where it runs.
[02:30] Erik Lund: We need “only EU” enforced, not “best effort.” And we need a statement that support access from outside EU is controlled.
[02:38] Marcus Lin: Yep. For private/VPC we can enforce that the data plane is within your network boundary, and support access is via approved break-glass with audit logs. For hosted, support access is also controlled and audited, but the strictest posture is private.

[03:02] Mikko Saarinen: On private: is it like fully on-prem? Or VPC? We’re not doing on-prem right now but VPC is possible.
[03:10] Marissa Cole: Private is usually VPC. On-prem is an option, but it’s heavier. VPC gives you private networking, your KMS integration, and we can deploy in your selected EU cloud region.

[03:25] Priya Nair: Let’s drill into “retention minimal.” What is the default retention for operational logs, and can we make it 7 days, for example?
[03:34] Allison Grant: For hosted, we have standard operational retention windows—varies by log type—but we can configure reduced retention for enterprise plans, and we can also route logs to your SIEM and keep less on our side. For private, you control the logging sinks more directly.
[03:53] Priya Nair: Do you have a “no log of payload” mode? Like, never store request body.
[03:58] Allison Grant: Yes, we can disable body logging. The system still emits metrics like token counts, latency, error codes, region, model ID. But not prompt text.
[04:10] Erik Lund: Token counts are still data. Are they linked to a user?
[04:15] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Our metering is keyed to API keys / org IDs and request IDs. We do not require end-user identifiers. If you pass a user ID, we treat it as a tag and we recommend hashing or not sending it. In private, you can enforce that at the gateway.

[04:35] Sanna Kivinen: We also need to understand where embeddings are stored. Some vendors keep embeddings for caching.
[04:42] Marissa Cole: We do caching at different layers. For embeddings, if you use our embeddings endpoint, the output is returned to you, we don’t store it as a database for retrieval. There are optional caches for performance—prefix/KV cache in runtime is ephemeral, in-memory, and tied to serving efficiency, not long-term storage.
[05:02] Erik Lund: KV cache is in memory on GPU?
[05:04] Marissa Cole: Yes, in-memory on the serving nodes. It’s not like a persistent store.
[05:10] Priya Nair: But you do store some request metadata, you said.
[05:13] Marcus Lin: Correct. Things like timestamps, model identifier, region, token counts, latency, error status—those are necessary for operating and billing. We can minimize and control retention.

[05:28] Sanna Kivinen: Ok. Next: residency. If we do hosted in EU, do you ever fail over to US during capacity issues?
[05:36] Marissa Cole: If you set policy to EU-only, we don’t route outside that boundary. There may be degraded performance rather than cross-region failover. In dedicated/private, it’s even more explicit.
[05:48] Sanna Kivinen: Good, we prefer fail-closed rather than fail-open.

[06:00] Erik Lund: Let’s talk identity and access. SSO, SAML, RBAC, audit logs.
[06:05] Kaitlyn Nguyen: For the Console, we support SSO via SAML for enterprise. RBAC includes roles for read-only, operator, admin, and we can scope by project/org. We emit audit events for login, role changes, API key operations, and access to sensitive pages.
[06:26] Erik Lund: Is audit log export possible to our SIEM?
[06:29] Kaitlyn Nguyen: Yes, we have export options and webhooks; for private we can integrate more directly. We’ll send a schema sample.

[06:42] Priya Nair: I want to flag: any audit logs that include prompts are a problem.
[06:47] Allison Grant: Agreed. Our audit logs are about control plane actions, not payload data. For request tracing, we can keep it payload-free.

[07:00] Mikko Saarinen: We also have internal governance where we need dashboards by region. Like consumption by region, model, and environment. Can Redwood provide that?
[07:10] Marissa Cole: Yes, at least at an aggregated level. We can show usage and performance broken down by region and model. We also have internal tooling around unit cost, which is grouped by model/region/tier.
[07:24] Sanna Kivinen: “Tier” meaning what exactly?

[07:47] Allison Grant: For compliance evidence, we can provide region-scoped metrics and logs. For cost governance, there’s a separate view internally that computes blended cost per output token by region and tier. 
[08:00] Priya Nair: Wait. You compute cost per output token? Is that customer visible?

[08:35] Erik Lund: Back to retention. We need deletion commitments. If we send a request, can you delete it immediately?

[09:00] Priya Nair: “Billing” is not an excuse to keep everything. You can bill off token counts without storing content.
[09:06] Marcus Lin: Agreed. We’re not arguing for content retention. Billing is based on metered tokens, not prompt text.

[09:58] Priya Nair: Can you confirm you don’t use prompts for training? Some providers have “improve service” toggles.
[10:04] Marcus Lin: Correct, we do not train foundation models on customer data. Any quality improvements happen via synthetic test sets and internal evaluation harnesses. We can put this in writing.
